Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

attachment.content:
- skills: Reference codebase for Crates. Use this skill when you need to understand the structure, implementation patterns, or code details of the Crates project.
- mcp-server-dev:build-mcp-app: This skill should be used when the user wants to build an "MCP app", add "interactive UI" or "widgets" to an MCP server, "render components in chat", build "MCP UI resources", make a tool that shows a "form", "picker", "dashboard" or "confirmation dialog" inline in the conversation, or mentions "apps SDK" in the context of MCP. Use AFTER the build-mcp-server skill has settled the deployment model, or when the user already knows they want UI widgets.
- mcp-server-dev:build-mcp-server: This skill should be used when the user asks to "build an MCP server", "create an MCP", "make an MCP integration", "wrap an API for Claude", "expose tools to Claude", "make an MCP app", or discusses building something with the Model Context Protocol. It is the entry point for MCP server development — it interrogates the user about their use case, determines the right deployment model (remote HTTP, MCPB, local stdio), picks a tool-design pattern, and hands off to specialized skills.
- mcp-server-dev:build-mcpb: This skill should be used when the user wants to "package an MCP server", "bundle an MCP", "make an MCPB", "ship a local MCP server", "distribute a local MCP", discusses ".mcpb files", mentions bundling a Node or Python runtime with their MCP server, or needs an MCP server that interacts with the local filesystem, desktop apps, or OS and must be installable without the user having Node/Python set up.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by running the app and observing behavior. Use when asked to verify a PR, confirm a fix works, test a change manually, check that a feature works, or validate local changes before pushing.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

2	# Provision a workspace subscriber — full container + memory setup.
3	#
4	# Creates an Incus container, configures networking, provisions memory
5	# namespaces and feature flags. This is the template run at signup.
6	#
7	# Identity chain: MAC address (user-provided shared key) -> WG keypair ->
8	#   full pubkey stored in CozoDB -> MCP token = UUID v5(pubkey).
9	# The MAC is less identifying than IP but hardware-bound to the user.
10	#
11	# Email is stored ONLY when GhostBridge is disabled. GhostBridge users
12	# route through the privacy layer and must not have email in CozoDB.
13	#
14	# Usage:
15	#   sudo ./provision-workspace-subscriber.sh <username> --mac <aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff> --psk <key> [--email <addr>] [--ghostbridge] [--semantic]
16	#
17	set -eu
18	
19	USERNAME="${1:?username required}"
20	shift
21	
22	MAC_ADDR=""
23	PSK=""
24	EMAIL=""
25	GHOSTBRIDGE=false
26	SEMANTIC=false
27	while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do
28	    case "$1" in
29	        --mac)         shift; MAC_ADDR="${1:?--mac requires a MAC address}" ;;
30	        --psk)         shift; PSK="${1:?--psk requires a pre-shared key}" ;;
31	        --email)       shift; EMAIL="${1:?--email requires an address}" ;;
32	        --ghostbridge) GHOSTBRIDGE=true ;;
33	        --semantic)    SEMANTIC=true ;;

35	    esac
36	    shift
37	done

39	CONTAINER_ID="ws-${USERNAME}"
40	IMAGE="images:debian/12"
41	MCP="http://100.90.37.254:3003/mcp"
42	
43	echo "=== Provisioning workspace subscriber: $USERNAME ==="

45	echo "    MAC address: ${MAC_ADDR:-<not provided>}"
46	echo "    PSK        : ${PSK:+<provided>}${PSK:-<not provided>}"
47	echo "    Email      : ${EMAIL:-<not provided>}"
48	echo "    GhostBridge: $GHOSTBRIDGE"
49	echo "    Semantic   : $SEMANTIC"
50	echo ""
51	
52	# ── 1. Create Incus container ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
53	echo "[1] Creating container..."
54	if incus info "$CONTAINER_ID" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
55	    echo "    Already exists — skipping"
56	else
57	    incus launch "$IMAGE" "$CONTAINER_ID"
58	    echo "    Launched $CONTAINER_ID"
59	fi
60	
61	# Wait for container to be ready
62	echo "    Waiting for init..."
63	sleep 3
64	incus exec "$CONTAINER_ID" -- sh -c "until [ -f /run/systemd/private ] || [ -d /run/s6 ] || pgrep -x init >/dev/null 2>&1 || sleep 1; do sleep 1; done" 2>/dev/null || sleep 2
65	
66	# ── 2. Base packages ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
67	echo "[2] Installing base packages..."
68	incus exec "$CONTAINER_ID" -- apt-get update -qq
69	incus exec "$CONTAINER_ID" -- apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
70	    curl ca-certificates wireguard-tools iproute2 \
71	    nodejs npm 2>/dev/null || true
72	
73	# ── 3. WireGuard identity — always provisioned ─────────────────────────────────
74	# The WG pubkey IS the identity. The MCP token is a UUID v5 derivative.
75	# The full pubkey is stored in the user database (CozoDB).
76	echo "[3] Generating WireGuard identity..."
77	incus exec "$CONTAINER_ID" -- sh -c "
78	    mkdir -p /etc/wireguard
79	    wg genkey | tee /etc/wireguard/privkey | wg pubkey > /etc/wireguard/pubkey
80	    chmod 600 /etc/wireguard/privkey
81	"
82	PEER_PUBKEY=$(incus exec "$CONTAINER_ID" -- cat /etc/wireguard/pubkey)
83	echo "    Peer pubkey: $PEER_PUBKEY"

86	TOKEN=$(uuidgen -v5 -n @oid -N "$PEER_PUBKEY")
87	echo "    MCP token : $TOKEN (derived from pubkey)"

138	    remember "container:${CONTAINER_ID}:identity" "email" \

140	fi

142	# Soul

162	# ── 6. Summary ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

#!/bin/sh
# Provision a workspace subscriber — full container + memory setup.
#
# Creates an Incus container, configures networking, provisions memory
# namespaces and feature flags. This is the template run at signup.
#
# Identity chain: MAC address (user-provided shared key) -> WG keypair ->
#   full pubkey stored in CozoDB -> MCP token = UUID v5(pubkey).
# The MAC is less identifying than IP but hardware-bound to the user.
#
# Email is stored ONLY when GhostBridge is disabled. GhostBridge users
# route through the privacy layer and must not have email in CozoDB.
#
# Usage:
#   sudo ./provision-workspace-subscriber.sh <username> --mac <aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff> --psk <key> [--email <addr>] [--ghostbridge] [--semantic]
#
set -eu

USERNAME="${1:?username required}"
shift

MAC_ADDR=""
PSK=""
EMAIL=""
GHOSTBRIDGE=false
SEMANTIC=false
while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do
    case "$1" in
        --mac)         shift; MAC_ADDR="${1:?--mac requires a MAC address}" ;;
        --psk)         shift; PSK="${1:?--psk requires a pre-shared key}" ;;
        --email)       shift; EMAIL="${1:?--email requires an address}" ;;
        --ghostbridge) GHOSTBRIDGE=true ;;
        --semantic)    SEMANTIC=true ;;
        *) echo "Unknown option: $1" >&2; exit 1 ;;
    esac
    shift
done

CONTAINER_ID="ws-${USERNAME}"
IMAGE="images:debian/12"
MCP="http://100.90.37.254:3003/mcp"

echo "=== Provisioning workspace subscriber: $USERNAME ==="
echo "    Container  : $CONTAINER_ID"
echo "    MAC address: ${MAC_ADDR:-<not provided>}"
echo "    PSK        : ${PSK:+<provided>}${PSK:-<not provided>}"
echo "    Email      : ${EMAIL:-<not provided>}"
echo "    GhostBridge: $GHOSTBRIDGE"
echo "    Semantic   : $SEMANTIC"
echo ""

# ── 1. Create Incus container ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
echo "[1] Creating container..."
if incus info "$CONTAINER_ID" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    echo "    Already exists — skipping"
else
    incus launch "$IMAGE" "$CONTAINER_ID"
    echo "    Launched $CONTAINER_ID"
fi

# Wait for container to be ready
echo "    Waiting for init..."
sleep 3
incus exec "$CONTAINER_ID" -- sh -c "until [ -f /run/systemd/private ] || [ -d /run/s6 ] || pgrep -x init >/dev/null 2>&1 || sleep 1; do sleep 1; done" 2>/dev/null || sleep 2

# ── 2. Base packages ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
echo "[2] Installing base packages..."
incus exec "$CONTAINER_ID" -- apt-get update -qq
incus exec "$CONTAINER_ID" -- apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    curl ca-certificates wireguard-tools iproute2 \
    nodejs npm 2>/dev/null || true

# ── 3. WireGuard identity — always provisioned ─────────────────────────────────
# The WG pubkey IS the identity. The MCP token is a UUID v5 derivative.
# The full pubkey is stored in the user database (CozoDB).
echo "[3] Generating WireGuard identity..."
incus exec "$CONTAINER_ID" -- sh -c "
    mkdir -p /etc/wireguard
    wg genkey | tee /etc/wireguard/privkey | wg pubkey > /etc/wireguard/pubkey
    chmod 600 /etc/wireguard/privkey
"
PEER_PUBKEY=$(incus exec "$CONTAINER_ID" -- cat /etc/wireguard/pubkey)
echo "    Peer pubkey: $PEER_PUBKEY"

# Derive MCP bearer token: UUID v5 from WG pubkey (one-way, not the raw key)
TOKEN=$(uuidgen -v5 -n @oid -N "$PEER_PUBKEY")
echo "    MCP token : $TOKEN (derived from pubkey)"

# GhostBridge networking (optional WG peer registration)
if [ "$GHOSTBRIDGE" = "true" ]; then
    echo "    GhostBridge: registering WireGuard peer..."
    # TODO: register peer with Netmaker API
    echo "    (Netmaker registration: TODO — wire to Netmaker API)"
else
    echo "    GhostBridge: skipped (networking only — identity already provisioned)"
fi

# ── 4. Semantic search — Qdrant collection ────────────────────────────────────
if [ "$SEMANTIC" = "true" ]; then
    echo "[4] Semantic search: enabled — Qdrant collection will be created on first use"
else
    echo "[4] Semantic search: skipped (disabled)"
fi

# ── 5. Memory namespaces via cognitive-mcp ────────────────────────────────────
echo "[5] Provisioning memory namespaces..."

remember() {
    NS="$1"; KEY="$2"; VAL="$3"
    RESULT=$(curl -sf -X POST "$MCP" \
        -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
        -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
        -H "User-Agent: op-dbus/1.0" \
        -d "{\"jsonrpc\":\"2.0\",\"id\":1,\"method\":\"tools/call\",\"params\":{\"name\":\"cognitive_memory\",\"arguments\":{\"operation\":\"store\",\"namespace\":\"$NS\",\"key\":\"$KEY\",\"value\":$VAL}}}" 2>&1) \
        && echo "    ok: $NS/$KEY" \
        || echo "    WARN: could not write $NS/$KEY (cognitive-mcp may be unreachable)"
}

NOW=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)

# Identity — cryptographic + hardware keys in CozoDB
remember "container:${CONTAINER_ID}:identity" "wireguard_pubkey" \
    "\"$PEER_PUBKEY\""
remember "container:${CONTAINER_ID}:identity" "mcp_token" \
    "\"$TOKEN\""
if [ -n "$MAC_ADDR" ]; then
    remember "container:${CONTAINER_ID}:identity" "mac_address" \
        "\"$MAC_ADDR\""
fi
if [ -n "$PSK" ]; then
    remember "container:${CONTAINER_ID}:identity" "psk" \
        "\"$PSK\""
fi

# Email: store ONLY when GhostBridge is disabled.
# GhostBridge users route through the privacy layer — email must not leak into CozoDB.
if [ -n "$EMAIL" ] && [ "$GHOSTBRIDGE" = "false" ]; then
    remember "container:${CONTAINER_ID}:identity" "email" \
        "\"$EMAIL\""
fi

# Soul
remember "container:${CONTAINER_ID}:soul" "profile" \
    "{\"kind\":\"soul\",\"container_id\":\"$CONTAINER_ID\",\"username\":\"$USERNAME\",\"created_at\":\"$NOW\"}"

# Domains
for DOMAIN in work personal home; do
    remember "container:${CONTAINER_ID}:domain:${DOMAIN}" "MEMORY_INDEX" \
        "{\"kind\":\"domain\",\"domain\":\"$DOMAIN\",\"container_id\":\"$CONTAINER_ID\",\"entries\":[]}"
done

# Index
remember "container:${CONTAINER_ID}:index" "MEMORY_INDEX" \
    "{\"kind\":\"index\",\"container_id\":\"$CONTAINER_ID\",\"namespaces\":[\"identity\",\"soul\",\"domain:work\",\"domain:personal\",\"domain:home\"]}"

# Feature flags
remember "container:${CONTAINER_ID}:features" "ghostbridge" \
    "{\"enabled\":$GHOSTBRIDGE}"
remember "container:${CONTAINER_ID}:features" "semantic_search" \
    "{\"enabled\":$SEMANTIC}"

# ── 6. Summary ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
echo ""
echo "=== Done ==="
echo ""
incus list "$CONTAINER_ID" 2>/dev/null || true
echo ""
echo "Identity:"
echo "  WG pubkey : $PEER_PUBKEY"
echo "  MCP token : $TOKEN (UUID v5 derivative)"
if [ -n "$MAC_ADDR" ]; then
echo "  MAC addr  : $MAC_ADDR (shared key)"
fi
if [ -n "$PSK" ]; then
echo "  PSK       : <stored>"
fi
if [ -n "$EMAIL" ] && [ "$GHOSTBRIDGE" = "false" ]; then
echo "  Email     : $EMAIL"
elif [ "$GHOSTBRIDGE" = "true" ]; then
echo "  Email     : <withheld — GhostBridge privacy>"
fi
echo ""
echo "Memory namespaces:"
echo "  container:${CONTAINER_ID}:identity"
echo "  container:${CONTAINER_ID}:soul"
echo "  container:${CONTAINER_ID}:domain:work"
echo "  container:${CONTAINER_ID}:domain:personal"
echo "  container:${CONTAINER_ID}:domain:home"
echo "  container:${CONTAINER_ID}:index"
echo "  container:${CONTAINER_ID}:features"
echo ""
echo "To enable GhostBridge:    sudo $0 $USERNAME --mac $MAC_ADDR --psk <key> --ghostbridge"
echo "To enable semantic search: sudo $0 $USERNAME --mac $MAC_ADDR --semantic"
echo "To enter container:        incus exec $CONTAINER_ID -- bash"

content.text:
Found it. `deploy/scripts/provision-workspace-subscriber.sh` is the template — its header literally says *"This is the template run at signup."*

## The provisioned-container template

**What it does**, in order:

1. **Creates the Incus container** — `incus launch images:debian/12 ws-<username>` (idempotent: skips if `ws-<username>` already exists), then waits for init (systemd/s6/init).
2. **Base packages** — `curl ca-certificates wireguard-tools iproute2 nodejs npm`.
3. **WireGuard identity (always)** — generates a keypair inside the container; the **pubkey is the identity**, and the **MCP bearer token is `uuidgen -v5` derived from that pubkey** (one-way, so the raw key never travels). GhostBridge peer registration with Netmaker is still a **TODO** (line 92-93).
4. **Semantic search (optional `--semantic`)** — no-op at provision time; Qdrant collection created lazily on first use.
5. **Memory namespaces** — POSTs to cognitive-mcp (`http://100.90.37.254:3003/mcp`) to seed `identity`, `soul`, `domain:{work,personal,home}`, `index`, and `features` namespaces.

**Identity chain** (header comment): `MAC (user-shared key) → WG keypair → full pubkey in CozoDB → MCP token = UUID v5(pubkey)`.

**Privacy rule to note:** email is stored in CozoDB **only when GhostBridge is disabled** (lines 137, 177-181). GhostBridge users route through the privacy layer and must not have email persisted.

```
sudo ./provision-workspace-subscriber.sh <username> \
  --mac <aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff> --psk <key> [--email <addr>] [--ghostbridge] [--semantic]
```

### How this relates to the magic-link registration you were just looking at

There are effectively **two separate registration paths that don't share an identity model**:

| | `op-web` signup (magic link) | `provision-workspace-subscriber.sh` |
|---|---|---|
| Identity | server-generated WG keypair, stored in CozoDB as `PrivacyUser` | container-generated WG keypair, pubkey → UUID v5 MCP token |
| Trigger | `POST /privacy/signup` → email magic link → `/privacy/verify` | manual CLI run "at signup" |
| Container | `ensure_host_privacy_network()` + container mapping in `users.rs` | `incus launch ws-<username>` |

The op-web handler (`privacy.rs:180`) calls `ensure_host_privacy_network()` but I don't see it invoking this provisioning script — so the magic-link web flow and this Incus template **aren't wired together yet**. The GhostBridge/Netmaker peer registration is also an open TODO in the script.

Want me to trace whether anything actually calls `provision-workspace-subscriber.sh` (e.g. from `privacy_network.rs` or a hook), to confirm whether the two paths are connected?

# op-identity Requirements

## Problem Statement
The Operation D-Bus system needs a robust, secure identity management layer capable of handling service and user identities, token-based authentication, and cryptographic keys.

## Functional Requirements

### FR-1: Service and User Identity
- Support unique identity representation for services and users.
- Provide a common `Identity` trait for all identity types.

### FR-2: Token-Based Authentication
- Support secure token generation, validation, and revocation.
- Integrate with `op-gateway` for WireGuard-based authentication.

### FR-3: Cryptographic Key Management
- Manage service and user cryptographic keys (X25519, Ed25519).
- Support secure key derivation and signing operations.

### FR-4: Integration and Monitoring
- Coordinate identity management with `op-api` for endpoint authentication.
- Integrate with `op-state-store` for persistent identity data.

## Non-Functional Requirements

### NFR-1: Performance
- < 10ms identity verification and token validation overhead.
- Minimal memory footprint for long-running identity processes.

### NFR-2: Scalability
- Efficiently scale across 1,000+ concurrent identities and tokens.
- Support high-throughput identity and token processing.

### NFR-3: Reliability
- Robust error handling and clear error messages.
- Automatic identity recovery and state persistence under failure scenarios.

### NFR-4: Security
- Secure identity data handling and encryption at rest if applicable.
- No memory leaks or resource exhaustion under high load.

# Spec — privacy-signup-container-provisioning

## Purpose

This document is the binding contract between the requirements, design decisions, and
implementation tasks for wiring the magic-link signup path to per-user Incus container
provisioning. It supersedes the `// TODO` comments in
`deploy/scripts/provision-workspace-subscriber.sh` lines ~90–96 and the unconnected
`ensure_user_container` call in `privacy.rs::provision_verified_user`.

---

## Scope

**In scope:**
- Triggering container provisioning as a background Tokio task after `verify_magic_link` succeeds.
- Injecting the server-side WireGuard keypair (already stored on `PrivacyUser`) into the Incus
  container — eliminating the divergent in-container keygen from the shell script.
- Deriving the MCP bearer token deterministically as `UUID v5(wg_public_key)` and persisting it.
- Seeding all nine cognitive-mcp memory namespace keys via `http://100.90.37.254:3003/mcp`.
- Registering the WireGuard peer with the Netmaker API when `ghostbridge_enabled = true`.
- Enforcing the email-privacy rule (no email in CozoDB or cognitive-mcp when GhostBridge is on).
- Adding `provisioning_status`, `mcp_token`, `ghostbridge_enabled`, `netmaker_peer_id`, and
  `provisioning_error` to `PrivacyUser` and CozoDB.
- Re-queuing `Pending`/`Provisioning` users at `AppState` startup.
- Unit and integration tests with all external calls mocked.

**Out of scope:**
- Changing the magic-link email delivery or SMTP configuration.
- Google OAuth handler changes (it picks up the new provisioner automatically).
- Per-user Qdrant collection initialisation (`--semantic` flag is seeded but collection
  creation is deferred).
- Container image selection (`images:debian/12` is fixed).
- Billing / quota enforcement logic.

---

## Architectural Constraints (binding)

| # | Constraint | Source |
|---|---|---|
| C-01 | No `Command::new("incus")` in Rust service code outside `IncusCliDriver`. | AGENTS.md §4 |
| C-02 | Server-side WireGuard keypair (`PrivacyUser.wg_public_key / wg_private_key_encrypted`) is the single identity source of truth. No keypair generated inside the container. | FR-3 |
| C-03 | Email must not appear in any CozoDB field or cognitive-mcp write when `ghostbridge_enabled = true`. | FR-6, NFR-3 |
| C-04 | `GET /privacy/verify` must return within 500 ms; provisioning is fire-and-forget. | NFR-1 |
| C-05 | MCP token derivation: `uuid::Uuid::new_v5(&Uuid::NAMESPACE_OID, pubkey.as_bytes())`. Matches `uuidgen -v5 -n @oid -N "$PEER_PUBKEY"`. | FR-3 |
| C-06 | All new source under `crates/op-web/src/`. No new crates, no `src/` at workspace root. | AGENTS.md §3 |
| C-07 | All new `subid` props registered in `op-plugins` OSCAL registry before merge. | AGENTS.md §4a |
| C-08 | WireGuard private keys must never appear in logs, HTTP responses, or structured events. | NFR-2 |

---

## Key Design Decisions

| Decision | Choice | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Provisioning trigger | `tokio::spawn` (fire-and-forget) after verify | Verify must return in < 500 ms; container launch can take 10–30 s. |
| Identity source of truth | Server-side keypair, injected into container | Avoids two divergent identities; server already owns the pubkey used for Netmaker and OpenFlow. |
| Incus interaction boundary | `IncusDriver` trait + `IncusCliDriver` impl | Allows mock injection in tests without spawning real containers; future-proofs a native REST driver. |
| Retry strategy | 3 attempts, 5 s / 15 s / 45 s backoff, on container launch and Netmaker API | Container cold-start is slow; Netmaker API can be transient. |
| `privacy_network_connected` | Retained as derived bool (`status == Ready`) | Backward compat for existing call sites and UI checks. |
| Email wipe on GhostBridge | `clear_user_email` mutates CozoDB row | Ensures the rule is enforced after the fact even if signup stored the email. |

---

## Acceptance Criteria

| ID | Criterion | Verified by |
|----|---|---|
| AC-01 | `GET /privacy/verify?token=<valid>` returns HTTP 200 in < 500 ms with `provisioning_status: "pending"`. | Integration test |
| AC-02 | After successful provisioning, `PrivacyUser.provisioning_status` is `Ready` and `privacy_container_name` is `ws-<user_id>`. | Integration test |
| AC-03 | Re-running provisioning on a `Ready` user is a no-op (no second container launch, no error). | Unit test |
| AC-04 | When `ghostbridge_enabled = true`, `PrivacyUser.email` is `""` in CozoDB and no `identity/email` write reaches cognitive-mcp. | Unit test with mock |
| AC-05 | When `ghostbridge_enabled = true` and Netmaker registration succeeds, `PrivacyUser.netmaker_peer_id` is non-empty. | Unit test with mock |
| AC-06 | When Netmaker API returns a non-2xx error, `provisioning_status` becomes `Failed` and `provisioning_error` contains the HTTP status. | Unit test with mock |
| AC-07 | Container WireGuard files `/etc/wireguard/privkey` and `/etc/wireguard/pubkey` match `PrivacyUser.wg_private_key_encrypted` and `wg_public_key`. | Integration test |
| AC-08 | `PrivacyUser.mcp_token` equals `uuid::Uuid::new_v5(&Uuid::NAMESPACE_OID, pubkey.as_bytes()).to_string()`. | Unit test |
| AC-09 | Users in `Pending`/`Provisioning` state at `AppState` startup are re-queued without human intervention. | Integration test |
| AC-10 | `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings` passes. | CI |
| AC-11 | `cargo test --workspace --all-targets --all-features` passes with 80 %+ coverage on `privacy_provisioner.rs`. | CI |

# Spec — zeroclaw-host-axum-schema-kiro

## Purpose
Deliver an Axum-backed gRPC / gRPC-Web host in `crates/op-grpc-bridge` that
surfaces the zeroclaw plugin schema to external consumers.  This spec is the
binding contract between requirements, design decisions, and implementation
tasks.

---

## Architectural Constraints (binding)

| # | Constraint | Source |
|---|-----------|--------|
| C-01 | `zeroclaw_schema()` in `plugin_schema_defs.rs` is the only schema definition. | AGENTS.md §2, FR-01 |
| C-02 | The Axum host reads schema from a plugin-owned file; it never generates or writes schema. | FR-02 |
| C-03 | Btrfs `@zeroclaw` subvolume is install/cache/rollback only; no D-Bus, projection, or OSCAL artefacts there. | FR-03 |
| C-04 | Native gRPC on Unix socket `/run/opdbus/zeroclaw-grpc.sock`. | FR-04 |
| C-05 | gRPC-Web + HTTP/1.1 on TCP via `tonic_web::enable`. | FR-05 |
| C-06 | D-Bus object `/org/opdbus/v1/services/zeroclaw_axum_host` is the config authority. | FR-06, AGENTS.md §4 |
| C-07 | All `subid` props registered in `op-plugins`; none defined in `op-grpc-bridge`. | FR-07, AGENTS.md §4a |
| C-08 | `X-Ghostbridge-Footprint` and `X-Ghostbridge-Trace-ID` stamped on every response. | FR-07, AGENTS.md §2 |
| C-09 | No Python; shell scripts only for deploy. | FR-08, AGENTS.md §4 |
| C-10 | No new `src/` at workspace root; all code under `crates/`. | AGENTS.md §3 |

---

## Interface Contract

### gRPC service: `zeroclaw.ZeroclawService`

| RPC | Request | Response | Stream |
|-----|---------|----------|--------|
| `GetSchema` | `GetSchemaRequest {}` | `SchemaResponse { schema_json, trace_id, footprint }` | unary |
| `WatchSchema` | `WatchSchemaRequest {}` | `SchemaEvent { schema_json, event_type }` | server-stream |

### D-Bus object: `/org/opdbus/v1/services/zeroclaw_axum_host`

| Property | Type | Access | Description |
|----------|------|--------|-------------|
| `BindAddr` | `String` | rw | TCP bind address (default `0.0.0.0:8090`) |
| `SchemaPath` | `String` | rw | Path to plugin-owned schema JSON |
| `ReloadIntervalSecs` | `u32` | rw | Periodic reload interval (0 = off) |
| `HealthStatus` | `String` | ro | `"ok"` or last error message |

### Schema file
- Path: `/dev/shm/opdbus/schemas/zeroclaw.json`
- Format: serialised `PluginSchema` JSON (canonical from `plugin_schema_defs.rs`)
- Written by: zeroclaw plugin
- Read by: `op-grpc-bridge` SchemaLoader

---

## Accepted Trade-offs

| Trade-off | Rationale |
|-----------|-----------|
| Axum host panics at startup if schema file absent | Plugin must start first; a soft fail would hide misconfigured s6 dependency. |
| Single `Arc<RwLock<…>>` for schema | Schema reloads are rare; contention is negligible. `DashMap` not needed. |
| No TLS on Unix socket | Loopback / same-host; TLS adds no security value on a UDS. |
| TCP endpoint unauthenticated by default | OpenClaw Trusted Proxy handles auth upstream; the Axum host is not the auth boundary. |

---

## Verification Criteria

| ID | Criterion | How to check |
|----|-----------|-------------|
| V-01 | `cargo clippy --workspace -D warnings` passes | CI |
| V-02 | `cargo fmt --all -- --check` passes | CI |
| V-03 | `cargo test --workspace --all-features` passes | CI |
| V-04 | `GetSchema` returns valid `PluginSchema` JSON matching zeroclaw plugin's schema | integration test |
| V-05 | `WatchSchema` emits `event_type: "reload"` within 1 s of `SIGHUP` | integration test |
| V-06 | D-Bus property `HealthStatus` returns `"ok"` after successful bind | manual / integration |
| V-07 | Response headers contain `X-Ghostbridge-Footprint` and `X-Ghostbridge-Trace-ID` | integration test |
| V-08 | gRPC-Web call from a browser-like HTTP/1.1 client succeeds | integration test |
| V-09 | Schema JSON on disk matches `zeroclaw_schema()` serialisation | unit test in `op-plugins` |

content.text:
Found the real picture inside wg-xray:
- The **only** thing running is `zeroclaw gateway start` (pid 132) on **:18789**.
- **Nothing is listening on `50051`** — the op-grpc-bridge that nginx proxies `assistant.3tched.com` to is **not running**.
- The container is **systemd-based**, so the gateway's stdout (the pairing code) is in **journald**, not a flat log file (that's why my earlier `/var/log` grep found nothing).

Pairing is **per-client**: even though `/health` says `paired:true`, a fresh browser must pair with the current one-time code. Let me pull it from journald.

echo; echo "=== fallback: any zeroclaw unit / how it was started ==="; sudo -n incus exec wg-xray -- sh -c 'systemctl status zeroclaw* 2>/dev/null | head -15; echo "---units---"; ls /etc/systemd/system/ 2>/dev/null | grep -i zero'

Now the model is clear. From `config.toml`:
- `require_pairing = true`, and there's already **one paired client** (`paired_tokens = ["enc2:…"]`).
- `[gateway.pairing_dashboard]`: codes are **8 chars** (`code_length = 8`), **expire after 1 hour** (`code_ttl_secs = 3600`), generated **on demand** (max 3 pending).

So the code isn't a static stored value — it's **minted on demand and printed to the gateway terminal**. The host codes you tried were 6-digit codes from a *different* instance, which is why they failed. You need to mint a fresh 8-char code from *this* gateway. Let me find the exact command.

**Mechanically yes, but there's nothing to import.** I tested the real path in wg-xray:

1	# Design — zeroclaw-host-axum-schema-kiro
2	
3	## 1. Crate Placement
4	
5	```
6	crates/
7	  op-plugins/            ← schema source of truth lives here
8	    src/state_plugins/
9	      plugin_schema_defs.rs   ← zeroclaw_schema() defined here
10	      zeroclaw.rs             ← calls Some(super::plugin_schema_defs::zeroclaw_schema())
11	  op-grpc-bridge/        ← new Axum host lives here
12	    src/
13	      lib.rs
14	      server.rs          ← Axum router + tonic-web setup
15	      schema_loader.rs   ← reads /dev/shm/opdbus/schemas/zeroclaw.json
16	      dbus_object.rs     ← registers /org/opdbus/v1/services/zeroclaw_axum_host
17	      grpc/
18	        zeroclaw.proto   ← generated from plugin schema; DO NOT hand-edit structs
19	        zeroclaw.rs      ← tonic generated (via build.rs)
20	      tracing.rs         ← X-Ghostbridge-Footprint injection middleware
21	```
22	
23	No `src/` at the workspace root. No schema definitions duplicated outside
24	`plugin_schema_defs.rs`.
25	
26	---
27	
28	## 2. Data-Flow: The Sled → Schema File → Axum Host
29	
30	```
31	 ┌─────────────────────┐
32	 │  SchemaEngine        │  (op-plugins, /dev/shm — The Sled)
33	 │  zeroclaw plugin     │
34	 │  schema() → JSON     │
35	 └────────┬────────────┘
36	          │ writes on startup / schema change
37	          ▼
38	 /dev/shm/opdbus/schemas/zeroclaw.json   ← plugin-owned file
39	          │
40	          │ reads at startup + SIGHUP (The Shuttle reads)
41	          ▼
42	 ┌─────────────────────┐
43	 │  op-grpc-bridge      │
44	 │  Axum host           │
45	 │  Arc<RwLock<Schema>> │
46	 └──────┬──────────────┘
47	        │
48	        ├──── Unix socket /run/opdbus/zeroclaw-grpc.sock  (native gRPC)
49	        └──── TCP 0.0.0.0:8090  (HTTP + gRPC-Web via tonic-web)
50	```
51	
52	**Btrfs is never in this path.** Btrfs (`@zeroclaw` subvolume) is only written
53	when the zeroclaw plugin commits a schema snapshot for rollback; the Axum host
54	has no Btrfs dependency.
55	
56	---
57	
58	## 3. Component Responsibilities
59	
60	### 3a. `op-plugins` (unchanged boundary)
61	- Owns `zeroclaw_schema()` in `plugin_schema_defs.rs`.
62	- Owns the OSCAL subid registry (all `subid` props).
63	- Writes `/dev/shm/opdbus/schemas/zeroclaw.json` via the plugin's own startup
64	  hook.
65	- Manages the Btrfs `@zeroclaw` subvolume for install/cache/rollback — no other
66	  crate touches it.
67	
68	### 3b. `op-grpc-bridge` — `schema_loader`
69	- `SchemaLoader` holds an `Arc<RwLock<serde_json::Value>>`.
70	- On startup: reads the plugin-owned JSON file. Panics with a clear message if
71	  the file is absent (plugin must start first).
72	- On `SIGHUP` (via `tokio::signal`): reloads within 50 ms.
73	- Never writes to `/dev/shm/opdbus/`.
74	
75	### 3c. `op-grpc-bridge` — `dbus_object`
76	- Connects to the system D-Bus.
77	- Exports `/org/opdbus/v1/services/zeroclaw_axum_host` with properties:
78	  - `BindAddr: String` (rw)
79	  - `SchemaPath: String` (rw)
80	  - `ReloadIntervalSecs: u32` (rw)
81	  - `HealthStatus: String` (ro)
82	- On `BindAddr` or `SchemaPath` write: triggers internal reload without process
83	  restart.
84	
85	### 3d. `op-grpc-bridge` — `server`
86	- Builds an `axum::Router` that:
87	  1. Mounts the tonic gRPC service at `/zeroclaw.ZeroclawService/…`
88	  2. Wraps it with `tonic_web::enable(…)` for gRPC-Web + HTTP/1.1 support.
89	  3. Applies `tower_http::cors::CorsLayer` with configurable origins.
90	  4. Runs `tracing` middleware that stamps every response with
91	     `X-Ghostbridge-Footprint` and `X-Ghostbridge-Trace-ID`.
92	- Binds two listeners concurrently via `tokio::join!`:
93	  - Unix socket (native gRPC)
94	  - TCP address (HTTP + gRPC-Web)
95	
96	### 3e. `op-grpc-bridge` — `tracing` middleware
97	- Extracts `X-Ghostbridge-Footprint` and `X-Ghostbridge-Trace-ID` from incoming
98	  request metadata (passed by OpenClaw Trusted Proxy).
99	- If absent, generates a new `Trace-ID` (UUID v7) and logs a warning.
100	- Injects both headers into response trailing metadata.
101	- Conforms to The Accountability Loop requirement.
102	
103	---
104	
105	## 4. Proto Contract
106	
107	```proto
108	// crates/op-grpc-bridge/src/grpc/zeroclaw.proto
109	syntax = "proto3";
110	package zeroclaw;
111	
112	// Schema is derived from PluginSchema; fields map 1:1 to zeroclaw_schema() keys.
113	// Re-generating this file requires running `cargo build` (build.rs invokes prost).
114	service ZeroclawService {
115	  rpc GetSchema    (GetSchemaRequest)    returns (SchemaResponse);
116	  rpc WatchSchema  (WatchSchemaRequest)  returns (stream SchemaEvent);
117	}
118	
119	message GetSchemaRequest  {}
120	message WatchSchemaRequest{}
121	
122	message SchemaResponse {
123	  string schema_json = 1;   // serialised PluginSchema JSON
124	  string trace_id    = 2;
125	  string footprint   = 3;
126	}
127	
128	message SchemaEvent {
129	  string schema_json = 1;
130	  string event_type  = 2;   // "initial" | "reload"
131	}
132	```
133	
134	`build.rs` invokes `tonic_build::compile_protos("src/grpc/zeroclaw.proto")`.
135	
136	---
137	
138	## 5. OSCAL Subid Assignments (all registered in `op-plugins`)
139	
140	| subid | what |
141	|-------|------|
142	| `src.service.zeroclaw-schema.file@v1` | plugin-owned JSON file in `/dev/shm` |
143	| `prj.service.zeroclaw-axum-host.bind@v1` | Axum server startup projection step |
144	| `obs.service.zeroclaw-schema.fetch@v1` | `GetSchema` RPC call |
145	| `obs.service.zeroclaw-schema.watch@v1` | `WatchSchema` streaming call |
146	| `mut.service.zeroclaw-axum-host.reload@v1` | SIGHUP / D-Bus triggered reload |
147	| `evt.service.zeroclaw-schema.reloaded@v1` | emitted after successful reload |
148	| `exp.service.zeroclaw-schema.grpc-web@v1` | tonic-web consumer surface |
149	
150	---
151	
152	## 6. Dependency Additions (`op-grpc-bridge/Cargo.toml`)
153	
154	New deps require PR justification per AGENTS.md §7. Pinned exact versions.
155	
156	| crate | version | justification |
157	|-------|---------|---------------|
158	| `tonic` | `=0.12.3` | gRPC transport; already in workspace |

168	| `anyhow` | `=1.0.93` | error handling |
169	| `tracing` | `=0.1.41` | structured logging |
170	| `tracing-subscriber` | `=0.3.19` | log formatting |
171	
172	---
173

175	
176	1. `op-plugins` starts → zeroclaw plugin D-Bus object published →
177	   `/dev/shm/opdbus/schemas/zeroclaw.json` written.

      zeroclaw.rs             ← calls Some(super::plugin_schema_defs::zeroclaw_schema())
  op-grpc-bridge/        ← new Axum host lives here
    src/
      lib.rs
      server.rs          ← Axum router + tonic-web setup
      schema_loader.rs   ← reads /dev/shm/opdbus/schemas/zeroclaw.json
      dbus_object.rs     ← registers /org/opdbus/v1/services/zeroclaw_axum_host
      grpc/
        zeroclaw.proto   ← generated from plugin schema; DO NOT hand-edit structs
        zeroclaw.rs      ← tonic generated (via build.rs)
      tracing.rs         ← X-Ghostbridge-Footprint injection middleware
```

No `src/` at the workspace root. No schema definitions duplicated outside
`plugin_schema_defs.rs`.

---

## 2. Data-Flow: The Sled → Schema File → Axum Host

```
 ┌─────────────────────┐
 │  SchemaEngine        │  (op-plugins, /dev/shm — The Sled)
 │  zeroclaw plugin     │
 │  schema() → JSON     │
 └────────┬────────────┘
          │ writes on startup / schema change
          ▼
 /dev/shm/opdbus/schemas/zeroclaw.json   ← plugin-owned file
          │
          │ reads at startup + SIGHUP (The Shuttle reads)
          ▼
 ┌─────────────────────┐
 │  op-grpc-bridge      │
 │  Axum host           │
 │  Arc<RwLock<Schema>> │
 └──────┬──────────────┘
        │
        ├──── Unix socket /run/opdbus/zeroclaw-grpc.sock  (native gRPC)
        └──── TCP 0.0.0.0:8090  (HTTP + gRPC-Web via tonic-web)
```

**Btrfs is never in this path.** Btrfs (`@zeroclaw` subvolume) is only written
when the zeroclaw plugin commits a schema snapshot for rollback; the Axum host
has no Btrfs dependency.

---

## 3. Component Responsibilities

### 3a. `op-plugins` (unchanged boundary)
- Owns `zeroclaw_schema()` in `plugin_schema_defs.rs`.
- Owns the OSCAL subid registry (all `subid` props).
- Writes `/dev/shm/opdbus/schemas/zeroclaw.json` via the plugin's own startup
  hook.
- Manages the Btrfs `@zeroclaw` subvolume for install/cache/rollback — no other
  crate touches it.

### 3b. `op-grpc-bridge` — `schema_loader`
- `SchemaLoader` holds an `Arc<RwLock<serde_json::Value>>`.
- On startup: reads the plugin-owned JSON file. Panics with a clear message if
  the file is absent (plugin must start first).
- On `SIGHUP` (via `tokio::signal`): reloads within 50 ms.
- Never writes to `/dev/shm/opdbus/`.

### 3c. `op-grpc-bridge` — `dbus_object`
- Connects to the system D-Bus.
- Exports `/org/opdbus/v1/services/zeroclaw_axum_host` with properties:
  - `BindAddr: String` (rw)
  - `SchemaPath: String` (rw)
  - `ReloadIntervalSecs: u32` (rw)
  - `HealthStatus: String` (ro)
- On `BindAddr` or `SchemaPath` write: triggers internal reload without process
  restart.

### 3d. `op-grpc-bridge` — `server`
- Builds an `axum::Router` that:
  1. Mounts the tonic gRPC service at `/zeroclaw.ZeroclawService/…`
  2. Wraps it with `tonic_web::enable(…)` for gRPC-Web + HTTP/1.1 support.
  3. Applies `tower_http::cors::CorsLayer` with configurable origins.
  4. Runs `tracing` middleware that stamps every response with
     `X-Ghostbridge-Footprint` and `X-Ghostbridge-Trace-ID`.
- Binds two listeners concurrently via `tokio::join!`:
  - Unix socket (native gRPC)
  - TCP address (HTTP + gRPC-Web)

### 3e. `op-grpc-bridge` — `tracing` middleware
- Extracts `X-Ghostbridge-Footprint` and `X-Ghostbridge-Trace-ID` from incoming
  request metadata (passed by OpenClaw Trusted Proxy).
- If absent, generates a new `Trace-ID` (UUID v7) and logs a warning.
- Injects both headers into response trailing metadata.
- Conforms to The Accountability Loop requirement.

---

## 4. Proto Contract

```proto
// crates/op-grpc-bridge/src/grpc/zeroclaw.proto
syntax = "proto3";
package zeroclaw;

// Schema is derived from PluginSchema; fields map 1:1 to zeroclaw_schema() keys.
// Re-generating this file requires running `cargo build` (build.rs invokes prost).
service ZeroclawService {
  rpc GetSchema    (GetSchemaRequest)    returns (SchemaResponse);
  rpc WatchSchema  (WatchSchemaRequest)  returns (stream SchemaEvent);
}

message GetSchemaRequest  {}
message WatchSchemaRequest{}

message SchemaResponse {
  string schema_json = 1;   // serialised PluginSchema JSON
  string trace_id    = 2;
  string footprint   = 3;
}

message SchemaEvent {
  string schema_json = 1;
  string event_type  = 2;   // "initial" | "reload"
}
```

`build.rs` invokes `tonic_build::compile_protos("src/grpc/zeroclaw.proto")`.

---

## 5. OSCAL Subid Assignments (all registered in `op-plugins`)

| subid | what |
|-------|------|
| `src.service.zeroclaw-schema.file@v1` | plugin-owned JSON file in `/dev/shm` |
| `prj.service.zeroclaw-axum-host.bind@v1` | Axum server startup projection step |
| `obs.service.zeroclaw-schema.fetch@v1` | `GetSchema` RPC call |
| `obs.service.zeroclaw-schema.watch@v1` | `WatchSchema` streaming call |
| `mut.service.zeroclaw-axum-host.reload@v1` | SIGHUP / D-Bus triggered reload |
| `evt.service.zeroclaw-schema.reloaded@v1` | emitted after successful reload |
| `exp.service.zeroclaw-schema.grpc-web@v1` | tonic-web consumer surface |

---

## 6. Dependency Additions (`op-grpc-bridge/Cargo.toml`)

New deps require PR justification per AGENTS.md §7. Pinned exact versions.

| crate | version | justification |
|-------|---------|---------------|
| `tonic` | `=0.12.3` | gRPC transport; already in workspace |
| `tonic-web` | `=0.12.3` | gRPC-Web + HTTP/1.1 bridge |
| `tonic-build` | `=0.12.3` | build-time proto compilation |
| `prost` | `=0.13.3` | protobuf runtime |
| `axum` | `=0.7.9` | HTTP router |
| `tower-http` | `=0.5.2` | CORS + tracing layers |
| `tokio` | `=1.40.0` | async runtime (features: full) |
| `serde_json` | `=1.0.133` | schema JSON handling |
| `zbus` | `=4.4.0` | D-Bus (already in workspace) |
| `uuid` | `=1.11.0` | trace-id generation (features: v7) |
| `anyhow` | `=1.0.93` | error handling |
| `tracing` | `=0.1.41` | structured logging |
| `tracing-subscriber` | `=0.3.19` | log formatting |

---

## 7. Startup Order

1. `op-plugins` starts → zeroclaw plugin D-Bus object published →
   `/dev/shm/opdbus/schemas/zeroclaw.json` written.
2. `op-grpc-bridge` starts → `SchemaLoader` reads JSON → D-Bus object registered
   → Axum server binds.
3. Clients connect to Unix socket (native gRPC) or TCP (gRPC-Web/HTTP).

S6 service definitions live in `deploy/s6/`.  `op-grpc-bridge` has a `needs`
dependency on `op-plugins`.

## Your question: subdomain?
**There is no subdomain mapped to this host yet.** The zeroclaw Axum host binds `0.0.0.0:8090` (gRPC + gRPC-Web), but nothing in `deploy/` routes a hostname to `:8090` — the only `8090` references are its own s6 run script and the subid-registry.

content.text:
Confirmed — and there's an important correction: the `unix_socket` plugin has **no imperative `create_socket(name, port)` method**. (`grep create_socket` → only OpenFlow's unrelated `create_socket_port`.) It's a **declarative** plugin: you add a `SocketEndpoint` entry to its `sockets` array and `apply_state`/`reconcile` binds it via `UnixListener::bind`.

## Exact syntax — `SocketEndpoint`

```json
{ "path": "/run/netmaker/mq.sock", "port": 1883, "protocol": "mqtt", "label": "netmaker-mqtt" }
```

| field | type | required | meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `path` | string | **yes** | socket filesystem path (this is the "name" — not a bare name) |
| `port` | u16 (1–65535) | **yes** | local TCP port xray listens on and proxies **into** the socket |
| `protocol` | string | no (default `"grpc"`) | `mqtt` / `http` / `grpc` / `jsonrpc` … |
| `label` | string | no | xray outbound tag (human label) |

So the call you remembered as `create_socket(name, port)` maps to `path` + `port` (plus `protocol`/`label`). The plugin reads desired state from `/dev/shm/live-schema.json` under key `unix_socket` → declares wholesale, no diff loop.

## For the netmaker broker specifically
The plugin's **own schema `example` already ships the exact broker entries** (`unix_socket.rs:522-555`):

```json
{ "path": "/run/netmaker/mq.sock",    "port": 1883, "protocol": "mqtt", "label": "netmaker-mqtt"  },
{ "path": "/run/netmaker/mqtts.sock", "port": 8883, "protocol": "mqtt", "label": "netmaker-mqtts" }
```

So the broker fix is to declare `/run/netmaker/mq.sock` → port 1883 (and `mqtts.sock` → 8883) in the `unix_socket` plugin state — **not** to call a method, and **not** to rebind mosquitto to `0.0.0.0`. Mosquitto stays loopback-only (as its config comment says: *"loopback only. Xray/Incus exposes tagged socket shims"*); xray bridges `1883` into the unix socket.

Want me to (a) just confirm what's currently declared in `/dev/shm/live-schema.json` for `unix_socket`, and/or (b) add the two netmaker broker entries to restore what kimi broke? I'll hold until you say which.

#!/bin/sh
# gbr-xray - Xray REALITY egress for GhostBridge privacy chain
# AGENTS.md: D-Bus-first architecture with accountability headers
#
# Dynamic cutover: prefer the schema-shuttle-generated config in /dev/shm;
# fall back to the static config until the shuttle has run at least once.

# Load secrets if available (XRAY_UUID, XRAY_PRIVATE_KEY, XRAY_SHORT_ID, NEXTDNS_PROFILE_ID)
if [ -f /etc/ghostbridge/xray.env ]; then
    . /etc/ghostbridge/xray.env
fi

DYNAMIC_CONFIG="/dev/shm/xray-ghostbridge.json"
STATIC_CONFIG="/etc/xray/config.json"

if [ -f "$DYNAMIC_CONFIG" ]; then
    XRAY_CONFIG="${XRAY_CONFIG:-$DYNAMIC_CONFIG}"
else
    XRAY_CONFIG="${XRAY_CONFIG:-$STATIC_CONFIG}"
fi

if [ ! -f "$XRAY_CONFIG" ]; then
    echo "Xray config not found: $XRAY_CONFIG"
    exit 0

The factory sessions answer your "how did it end up" question — and confirm your instinct it's **not** a simple proxy device, it's a **bidirectional pair**:

- **Broker side** (`netmaker-mq`): mosquitto loopback `1883` → incus proxy `mqtt-sock` *exports* it to host `/run/netmaker/mq.sock`.
- **Consumer side** (`netmaker` server): a **`bind: instance`** proxy `broker-1883` *re-imports* host `/run/netmaker/mq.sock` back as `tcp:127.0.0.1:1883` **inside** the netmaker container.

Session `a0cea9cd` was literally the droid asking "should a proxy device be added to the netmaker container to forward the broker connection, and what's the exact command" — that's where `broker-1883` came from.

To make it concrete, here's the one thing I'm actually unsure about: **a single Unix socket can only serve one listener**, so for *all* containers to share *one* socket, something has to demux the traffic to the right container. The three realistic ways that happens:

- **xray demuxes by SNI** — works only for TLS-wrapped traffic (the hostname is in the TLS ClientHello). Your `:443 sni-dispatch` already does exactly this; "one shared socket" would just move that front door from a TCP port to a single UDS.
- **A port/tag carried in the protocol** — needs every client to speak a framing that names the target. More custom.
- **It's really "one socket *per container*"** (collapsing the 4 netmaker sockets into 1), not literally one socket for the whole host.

2. Is the traffic through it **all TLS** (so SNI demux is viable), or mixed plaintext (mqtt/http) that has no SNI?
3. Is this the **ingress** front door (external → containers), or also egress?

content.text:
Good — that reframes it, and it makes the answer simpler.

## What "custom framing" is
It means putting a tiny header in front of each connection's bytes that says which container it's for — e.g. `[len][container-id][payload…]`. A mux process reads the tag, strips it, and forwards the rest to the right container. The problem: **nothing speaks it out of the box.** A browser, an MQTT client, grpc — none of them prepend your tag, so you'd need a shim on *both* ends translating in and out. It's the most code and the most fragile. **You don't want this.** I only listed it for completeness.

## You already have the right answer: demux by hostname, not by port
The "thousand ports" problem comes purely from the current design giving each service its **own redirect port** (`:21883`, `:28081`, `:28082`, …). That doesn't scale to a container-per-user. The fix is the thing xray is *already* doing on `:443` — **SNI dispatch**:

- One ingress (one port, or one UDS).
- The hostname rides in the TLS handshake (SNI) — readable without decrypting.
- Each user/container = **a subdomain** (`alice.ghostbridge.tech` → `ws-alice`), not a port.
- Adding a user adds **one routing rule**, not a port and not a socket.

```
        ONE socket/port (:443 sni-dispatch today)
                 │  read SNI hostname
   ┌─────────────┼─────────────────────────┐
 alice.gb.tech  bob.gb.tech   broker.gb.tech ...
   ▼             ▼               ▼
 ws-alice      ws-bob        netmaker-mq
```

So: **1 socket, N subdomains, 0 extra ports per user.** That's the scalable shape, and it's an extension of your existing `sni-dispatch`, not a rewrite.

## The one real design question that remains
With a container per user, you don't want to hand-write an outbound per user either. Two ways to keep it zero-touch:

1. **Generated routes (shm-reactive):** provisioning a user writes a route entry; the schema-shuttle regenerates `/dev/shm/xray-ghostbridge.json`. Still one port — you just get N cheap routing rules in shm, auto-managed. Matches your existing "shuttle writes shm" model.
2. **Dynamic resolve on connect:** the ingress reads SNI `alice.…` → derives container `ws-alice` → connects to its socket/IP at connection time. No per-user config at all. (This is the "xray greets connections, no polling" idea from the factory handoff — but xray core can't do arbitrary dynamic backends, so this one needs a small resolver in front.)

One caveat: **SNI demux needs TLS.** Plaintext MQTT (`1883`) has no SNI, so the broker either goes over MQTT-in-TLS (`8883`, SNI works) or stays a fixed internal route. Everything user-facing (HTTPS/gRPC-Web/WSS) is TLS, so it's fine there.

Before I sketch the concrete change: do you want **(1) generated routes from the schema** (fits your shm/shuttle architecture, less new code) or **(2) a dynamic SNI resolver** (zero per-user config, but a new small front-end component)? I'd recommend **(1)**.

---
name: xray-native-unix-socket-routing
description: Shared-ingress design for per-user containers — xray routes natively to unix sockets, so no per-user TCP ports
metadata:
  type: project
---

For the GhostBridge / operation-dbus-proto shared-ingress architecture (container per user, `ws-<user>`): **xray can route directly to unix domain sockets natively** — an outbound can dial a UDS path, no intermediate TCP listener needed.

**Why this matters:** it kills the "thousand ports" problem. The current live `/etc/xray/config.json` uses per-service TCP redirects (`netmaker-mq-out → 127.0.0.1:21883`, `netmaker-api-out → :28081`, `netmaker-ui-out → :28082`, `assistant-out → :18789`). Those dedicated ports don't scale to a container-per-user. The target design: **one shared ingress (SNI dispatch on `:443`, already exists) → route by subdomain → outbound that dials the container's unix socket at `path` directly.** Per user = one subdomain + one route, zero new ports/sockets.

**The `unix_socket` plugin** (`crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/unix_socket.rs`) declares the endpoints. Schema is schemars-derived from `UnixSocketState { sockets: Vec<SocketEndpoint> }`. `SocketEndpoint` fields: `path` (req), `port` (req, u16 1-65535), `protocol` (default "grpc"), `label` (= xray outbound tag). It is **declarative, not imperative** — no `create_socket(name, port)` method; you add an entry to the `sockets` array and `apply_state`/`reconcile` binds it via `UnixListener::bind`. Desired state is read from `/dev/shm/live-schema.json` under key `unix_socket`. The plugin's own schema `example` already ships the netmaker entries (`/run/netmaker/mq.sock` port 1883, `mqtts.sock` 8883, `api.sock` 8081, `ui.sock` 80).

**Tension to resolve at implementation:** `SocketEndpoint.port` is documented as "Local TCP port xray listens on and proxies into this socket" — the legacy TCP-shim model. If xray dials the UDS directly, that TCP-listen step (and the per-user port) is what we're eliminating, so `port` becomes vestigial/a hint. Confirm exact xray UDS config form (Domain Socket / dialing `path`) when wiring.

Related: [[unix-socket-plugin]] design; SNI demux requires TLS (plaintext mqtt 1883 has no SNI → use 8883 or a fixed internal route).

Saved. Internalized — here's what xray's native UDS routing collapses:

## The whole TCP-port layer disappears
Right now every service has a dedicated redirect port:
```
netmaker-mq-out  → 127.0.0.1:21883
netmaker-api-out → 127.0.0.1:28081
netmaker-ui-out  → 127.0.0.1:28082
assistant-out    → 127.0.0.1:18789
```
With xray dialing the socket directly, those become:
```
broker.*    → /run/netmaker/mq.sock      (no :21883)
api.*       → /run/netmaker/api.sock     (no :28081)
dashboard.* → /run/netmaker/ui.sock      (no :28082)
alice.*     → /run/ws/alice.sock         ← per user, just a path
```

So the model is: **one ingress (`:443` SNI) → demux by subdomain → dial the container's unix socket by path.** Per user = one subdomain + one `SocketEndpoint` entry. **Zero ports added per container.** That's exactly the no-thousand-ports outcome.

Two code spots currently assume filesystem sockets and must change:
- `schema_bridge.rs:714-715` hardcodes `"abstract": false` with `/run/…` paths → set `abstract: true`, abstract name.

name: xray-native-unix-socket-routing
description: "Shared-ingress design for per-user containers — xray routes natively to unix sockets, so no per-user TCP ports"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: df5b94d0-cefa-43d0-9f9d-c4cea5de8d65
---

For the GhostBridge / operation-dbus-proto shared-ingress architecture (container per user, `ws-<user>`): **xray can route directly to unix domain sockets natively** — an outbound can dial a UDS path, no intermediate TCP listener needed.

**Why this matters:** it kills the "thousand ports" problem. The current live `/etc/xray/config.json` uses per-service TCP redirects (`netmaker-mq-out → 127.0.0.1:21883`, `netmaker-api-out → :28081`, `netmaker-ui-out → :28082`, `assistant-out → :18789`). Those dedicated ports don't scale to a container-per-user. The target design: **one shared ingress (SNI dispatch on `:443`, already exists) → route by subdomain → outbound that dials the container's unix socket at `path` directly.** Per user = one subdomain + one route, zero new ports/sockets.

**The `unix_socket` plugin** (`crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/unix_socket.rs`) declares the endpoints. Schema is schemars-derived from `UnixSocketState { sockets: Vec<SocketEndpoint> }`. `SocketEndpoint` fields: `path` (req), `port` (req, u16 1-65535), `protocol` (default "grpc"), `label` (= xray outbound tag). It is **declarative, not imperative** — no `create_socket(name, port)` method; you add an entry to the `sockets` array and `apply_state`/`reconcile` binds it via `UnixListener::bind`. Desired state is read from `/dev/shm/live-schema.json` under key `unix_socket`. The plugin's own schema `example` already ships the netmaker entries (`/run/netmaker/mq.sock` port 1883, `mqtts.sock` 8883, `api.sock` 8081, `ui.sock` 80).

**Tension to resolve at implementation:** `SocketEndpoint.port` is documented as "Local TCP port xray listens on and proxies into this socket" — the legacy TCP-shim model. If xray dials the UDS directly, that TCP-listen step (and the per-user port) is what we're eliminating, so `port` becomes vestigial/a hint. Confirm exact xray UDS config form (Domain Socket / dialing `path`) when wiring.

Related: [[unix-socket-plugin]] design; SNI demux requires TLS (plaintext mqtt 1883 has no SNI → use 8883 or a fixed internal route).

---
name: xray-native-unix-socket-routing
description: "Shared-ingress design for per-user containers — xray routes natively to unix sockets, so no per-user TCP ports"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: df5b94d0-cefa-43d0-9f9d-c4cea5de8d65
---

For the GhostBridge / operation-dbus-proto shared-ingress architecture (container per user, `ws-<user>`): **xray can route directly to unix domain sockets natively** — an outbound can dial a UDS path, no intermediate TCP listener needed.

**Why this matters:** it kills the "thousand ports" problem. The current live `/etc/xray/config.json` uses per-service TCP redirects (`netmaker-mq-out → 127.0.0.1:21883`, `netmaker-api-out → :28081`, `netmaker-ui-out → :28082`, `assistant-out → :18789`). Those dedicated ports don't scale to a container-per-user. The target design: **one shared ingress (SNI dispatch on `:443`, already exists) → route by subdomain → outbound that dials the container's unix socket directly.** Per user = one subdomain + one route, zero new ports/sockets.

**How xray dials the socket (already implemented):** `crates/op-identity/src/schema_bridge.rs` (`run_schema_shuttle` → writes `/dev/shm/xray-ghostbridge.json`) builds a per-socket `to-<label>` outbound using xray's native **`domainsocket`** transport: `streamSettings.network="domainsocket"`, `dsSettings.path=<path>`. SNI is sniffed at the shared REALITY/TLS ingress and a domain routing rule (`domain: [<subdomain>] → outboundTag to-<label>`) dials it. Declared via env `UNIX_SOCKET_ENDPOINTS=label:/path:subdomain[,…]` → `SocketEntry{label,path,domain}`, or `/dev/shm/xray-routes.json` (`GemmaBackend::Unix{path}`). No per-socket TCP inbound, no NIC.

**CORRECTION (user, authoritative):** the `unix_socket` plugin should create **ABSTRACT** namespace sockets ("dbus sockets" — named by D-Bus object-path convention, leading-null `@name`), NOT `/run/` filesystem sockets. xray dials them with `dsSettings.abstract = true`. Two code spots currently assume filesystem sockets and must change:
- `schema_bridge.rs:714-715` hardcodes `"abstract": false` with `/run/…` paths → set `abstract: true`, abstract name.
- `unix_socket.rs` `ensure_bound` does `create_dir_all(parent)` + `remove_file` + `UnixListener::bind(path)` (filesystem) → must bind an abstract socket instead (no `/run/` entry).
Goal: xray routes straight to the plugin-created abstract/dbus socket; nothing lands in `/run/`. The `/run/netmaker/*.sock` I saw are the LEGACY incus-proxy-device approach being replaced.

**The `unix_socket` plugin** (`crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/unix_socket.rs`) declares the endpoints. Schema is schemars-derived from `UnixSocketState { sockets: Vec<SocketEndpoint> }`. `SocketEndpoint` fields: `path` (req), `port` (req, u16 1-65535), `protocol` (default "grpc"), `label` (= xray outbound tag). It is **declarative, not imperative** — no `create_socket(name, port)` method; you add an entry to the `sockets` array and `apply_state`/`reconcile` binds it via `UnixListener::bind`. Desired state is read from `/dev/shm/live-schema.json` under key `unix_socket`. The plugin's own schema `example` already ships the netmaker entries (`/run/netmaker/mq.sock` port 1883, `mqtts.sock` 8883, `api.sock` 8081, `ui.sock` 80).

**Tension to resolve at implementation:** `SocketEndpoint.port` is documented as "Local TCP port xray listens on and proxies into this socket" — the legacy TCP-shim model. If xray dials the UDS directly, that TCP-listen step (and the per-user port) is what we're eliminating, so `port` becomes vestigial/a hint. Confirm exact xray UDS config form (Domain Socket / dialing `path`) when wiring.

**Domain routing is the mechanism (confirmed live + in generator), and it was a required switch:** with one shared port (`:443`), port/IP routing can't distinguish containers — every connection lands on the same listener. The only discriminator is the sniffed SNI hostname, so routing MUST be by `domain`. Live `/etc/xray/config.json` and `schema_bridge.rs` both set: every inbound `sniffing.enabled=true` + `destOverride:["tls","http","quic"]` + `routeOnly=true`; `routing.domainStrategy="AsIs"`; rules `{"type":"field","domain":[…],"outboundTag":"to-<label>"}`. `routeOnly:true` = use sniffed name only to pick the outbound, don't rewrite the destination. Adding a user = one domain rule + one `to-<label>` domainsocket outbound in `/dev/shm`, regenerated by the shuttle.

Related: [[unix-socket-plugin]] design; SNI demux requires TLS (plaintext mqtt 1883 has no SNI → use 8883 or a fixed internal route).

The dynamic config is now generating in shm and validates — but this also pinpoints **exactly** why you're still seeing ports instead of sockets.

## ✅ Done: dynamic xray conf generates in shm
```
op-gemma  → /dev/shm/xray-routes.json + openflow-routes.json
shuttle   → /dev/shm/xray-ghostbridge.json   (xray -test: "Configuration OK.")
```
Domain routing is correct — SNI → `to-<tag>`:
```
assistant.ghostbridge.tech  → to-grpc-bridge
broker.ghostbridge.tech     → to-netmaker-mq
api.ghostbridge.tech        → to-netmaker-api
dashboard.ghostbridge.tech  → to-netmaker-ui
qdrant.ghostbridge.tech     → to-qdrant
```

## ⚠️ But the backends are still legacy TCP ports, and here's the root cause
The generated outbounds are plain freedom redirects, **not** domainsocket:
```
to-netmaker-mq  → redirect 127.0.0.1:21883
to-netmaker-api → redirect 127.0.0.1:28081
to-netmaker-ui  → redirect 127.0.0.1:28082
to-qdrant       → redirect 127.0.0.1:6334
```
Because the **source — `/etc/ghostbridge/subid-registry.json` — declares them `"type":"tcp"`** with those ports. op-gemma faithfully turned `tcp` into TCP redirects. The shuttle *already* has the `GemmaBackend::Unix{path}` → `network:domainsocket` branch (`schema_bridge.rs:708`); it's just never exercised because nothing in the registry is `type:unix`.

So the "one socket, no thousand ports" change is a **single-source edit**: in the subid-registry, change those backend entries from
```json
{"type":"tcp","host":"127.0.0.1","port":21883}
```
to
```json
{"type":"unix","path":"<abstract socket name>"}
```
then re-run gemma+shuttle → domainsocket outbounds appear. Plus the `abstract:false→true` flip (`schema_bridge.rs:714`) for the no-`/run/` "dbus socket" form.

## State note
I only **generated** the file — I did **not** cut xray over. The running xray is unchanged. But heads-up: `gbr-xray` prefers the dynamic config when present, so its **next restart will load this one** — and it has a different inbound shape than the static (`op-tls:443` + `ghostbridge-reality:8443` only; no `:80`/`tls-h1`/`tls-h2`). 

Want me to:
1. **Convert the registry's `tcp` backends → `unix` (abstract)** and regenerate, so the dynamic config uses domainsocket/no-ports — the actual design? (I'll also wire the `abstract:true` flip.)
2. Or leave the registry as-is and just keep the TCP-based dynamic config you now have?

I'd go with **(1)** since that's the whole point. Confirm and I'll make the registry edit + regenerate (still no xray cutover until you say).

content.text:
Ground truth changes the plan — and confirms what kimi broke:

- The **`/run/` sockets all exist** and reach the services (`/run/netmaker/{mq,api,ui}.sock`, `/run/qdrant.sock`) — created by incus proxy devices.
- The **legacy TCP ports the registry points at are mostly DEAD**: nothing listens on `:21883`/`:28081`/`:28082` (only `:6334` is up). So the current registry → xray would dial **dead ports** — that's the broken broker routing.
- **No abstract service sockets exist** — incus proxy binds *filesystem* `/run/` sockets, and the `unix_socket` plugin isn't running as a forwarder. So pointing xray at an `abstract:true` socket right now would dial **nothing**.

So the correct, working version of option 1 is: registry `tcp` → `unix` pointing at the **existing `/run/` sockets** (`abstract:false`). That removes the dead TCP ports *and* fixes routing. Fully-abstract "no `/run/`" needs a producer that binds abstract sockets — a separate change with no backend today. Let me read the registry to edit precisely.

print("changed:")
for c in changed: print("  ",c)
PY

listen: address

The listening address, which can be an IP address or a Unix domain socket. The default value is "0.0.0.0", which means listening on all network interfaces.

You can specify an IP address available on the system.

"::" is equivalent to "0.0.0.0"; both will listen on IPv6 and IPv4 simultaneously. However, if you only want to listen on IPv6, you can set v6only in sockopt to true. If you only want to listen on IPv4, you can use commands like ip a to view the specific IP on the network card (usually the machine's public IP address or a private network address like 10.x.x.x) and listen on that. Of course, you can do the same for IPv6.

Note that because UDP is not connection-oriented, if the inbound is based on UDP and there are multiple IP addresses on the network card, and the external connection is to a non-preferred address on the card, Xray might incorrectly use the preferred address as the source address for the reply instead of the target of the external connection, causing the connection to fail. The solution is not to listen on 0.0.0.0 but to listen on the specific IP address on the network card.

Supports Unix domain sockets in absolute path format, such as "/dev/shm/domain.socket". You can add @ at the beginning to represent abstract, and @@ for abstract with padding.

When filling in a Unix domain socket, port and allocate will be ignored. The protocol can currently be VLESS, VMess, or Trojan, and applies only to TCP-based transport methods, such as tcp, websocket, grpc. UDP-based transports like mkcp are not supported.

When filling in a Unix domain socket, you can use the format "/dev/shm/domain.socket,0666", i.e., adding a comma and access permission indicators after the socket, to specify the access permissions of the socket. This can be used to solve socket permission issues that occur by default.

port: number | "env:variable" | string

Port. Accepted formats are as follows:

Integer value: The actual port number.
Environment variable: Starts with "env:", followed by the name of an environment variable, such as "env:PORT". Xray will parse this environment variable as a string.
String: Can be a numeric string, such as "1234"; or a numerical range, such as "5-10" indicating ports 5 to 10 (6 ports in total). Commas can be used for segmentation, such as 11,13,15-17 indicating port 11, port 13, and ports 15 to 17 (5 ports in total).
When only one port is specified, Xray will listen for inbound connections on this port. When a port range is specified, Xray will listen on all ports within the range.

Note that listening on a port is a relatively expensive operation. Listening on a port range that is too large may cause a significant increase in resource usage or even cause Xray to fail to work properly. Generally speaking, problems may begin to appear when the number of listening ports approaches four digits. If you need to use a very large range, please consider using iptables for redirection instead of setting it here.

protocol: "tunnel" | "http" | "shadowsocks" | "socks" | "vless" | "vmess" | "trojan" | "wireguard" | "hysteria" | "tun"

settings: InboundConfigurationObject

Specific configuration content, which varies by protocol. See InboundConfigurationObject in each protocol section for details.

streamSettings: StreamSettingsObject

Transport configuration for this inbound.

tag: string The identifier of this inbound connection, used to locate this connection in other configurations.

DANGER

sniffing: SniffingObject

Traffic sniffing is mainly used for transparent proxies and similar purposes. A typical flow is as follows:

If a device accesses the internet and visits abc.com, the device first queries DNS to get the IP of abc.com as 1.2.3.4, and then the device initiates a connection to 1.2.3.4.
If sniffing is not configured, the connection request received by Xray is for 1.2.3.4, which cannot be used for routing traffic based on domain rules.
When enabled in sniffing is set to true, Xray will sniff the domain name, i.e., abc.com, from the traffic data when processing this connection.
Xray will reset 1.2.3.4 to abc.com. The routing can then divert traffic according to the domain rules.
Because it becomes a connection requesting abc.com, more things can be done. Besides routing domain rule diversion, it can also re-perform DNS resolution and other tasks.

When enabled in sniffing is set to true, it can also sniff Bittorrent type traffic. Then you can configure the "protocol" item in routing to set rules for handling unencrypted BT traffic. For example, the server side can be used to intercept unencrypted BT traffic, or the client side can fixedly forward BT traffic to a certain VPS, etc.

Note: Newer browsers may use ECH to encrypt the Client Hello. In this case, Xray can only see the domain in the Outer Hello. You may need to consider hijacking DNS or manually disabling ECH in the browser configuration.

content.text:
Both things confirmed empirically, and they rewrite the plan:

## Verified facts (xray 26.3.27 on the host)
| Primitive | Result |
|---|---|
| **Outbound** `network:"domainsocket"` | ❌ removed — "unknown transport protocol" |
| **Outbound** `network:"unix"` | ❌ unknown |
| **Outbound** freedom `redirect` to a path | ❌ requires a port |
| **Inbound** `listen:"/dev/shm/x.sock"` | ✅ Configuration OK |
| **Inbound** `listen:"@ghostbridge/ingress"` (abstract = "dbus socket") | ✅ OK |
| **Inbound** `listen:"@@…"` (abstract+padding) | ✅ OK |
| **Inbound** `listen:"…sock,0666"` (perms) | ✅ OK |

So you were right that xray natively does unix/abstract sockets — but the primitive is **inbound `listen`**, not an outbound dial. That flips the implementation: the abstract "dbus socket" is a **socket xray listens on**, and the `schema_bridge.rs` code that generates a `domainsocket` **outbound** is the stale/broken part (it targets an xray version that still had that transport).

## Safety restored
I reverted the unsafe state: registry back to `tcp` (4 entries), and removed the generated `/dev/shm/xray-*.json` (which failed `xray -test`). `gbr-xray` now falls back to the known-good static `/etc/xray/config.json` — exactly the pre-session baseline. name: xray-native-unix-socket-routing
description: "Shared-ingress design for per-user containers — xray routes natively to unix sockets, so no per-user TCP ports"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project

For the GhostBridge / operation-dbus-proto shared-ingress architecture (container per user, `ws-<user>`): **xray can route directly to unix domain sockets natively** — an outbound can dial a UDS path, no intermediate TCP listener needed.

**Why this matters:** it kills the "thousand ports" problem. The current live `/etc/xray/config.json` uses per-service TCP redirects (`netmaker-mq-out → 127.0.0.1:21883`, `netmaker-api-out → :28081`, `netmaker-ui-out → :28082`, `assistant-out → :18789`). Those dedicated ports don't scale to a container-per-user. The target design: **one shared ingress (SNI dispatch on `:443`, already exists) → route by subdomain → outbound that dials the container's unix socket directly.** Per user = one subdomain + one route, zero new ports/sockets.

**How xray dials the socket (already implemented):** `crates/op-identity/src/schema_bridge.rs` (`run_schema_shuttle` → writes `/dev/shm/xray-ghostbridge.json`) builds a per-socket `to-<label>` outbound using xray's native **`domainsocket`** transport: `streamSettings.network="domainsocket"`, `dsSettings.path=<path>`. SNI is sniffed at the shared REALITY/TLS ingress and a domain routing rule (`domain: [<subdomain>] → outboundTag to-<label>`) dials it. Declared via env `UNIX_SOCKET_ENDPOINTS=label:/path:subdomain[,…]` → `SocketEntry{label,path,domain}`, or `/dev/shm/xray-routes.json` (`GemmaBackend::Unix{path}`). No per-socket TCP inbound, no NIC.

**CORRECTION (user, authoritative):** the `unix_socket` plugin should create **ABSTRACT** namespace sockets ("dbus sockets" — named by D-Bus object-path convention, leading-null `@name`), NOT `/run/` filesystem sockets. xray dials them with `dsSettings.abstract = true`. Two code spots currently assume filesystem sockets and must change:
- `schema_bridge.rs:714-715` hardcodes `"abstract": false` with `/run/…` paths → set `abstract: true`, abstract name.
- `unix_socket.rs` `ensure_bound` does `create_dir_all(parent)` + `remove_file` + `UnixListener::bind(path)` (filesystem) → must bind an abstract socket instead (no `/run/` entry).
Goal: xray routes straight to the plugin-created abstract/dbus socket; nothing lands in `/run/`. The `/run/netmaker/*.sock` I saw are the LEGACY incus-proxy-device approach being replaced.

**The `unix_socket` plugin** (`crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/unix_socket.rs`) declares the endpoints. Schema is schemars-derived from `UnixSocketState { sockets: Vec<SocketEndpoint> }`. `SocketEndpoint` fields: `path` (req), `port` (req, u16 1-65535), `protocol` (default "grpc"), `label` (= xray outbound tag). It is **declarative, not imperative** — no `create_socket(name, port)` method; you add an entry to the `sockets` array and `apply_state`/`reconcile` binds it via `UnixListener::bind`. Desired state is read from `/dev/shm/live-schema.json` under key `unix_socket`. The plugin's own schema `example` already ships the netmaker entries (`/run/netmaker/mq.sock` port 1883, `mqtts.sock` 8883, `api.sock` 8081, `ui.sock` 80).

**Tension to resolve at implementation:** `SocketEndpoint.port` is documented as "Local TCP port xray listens on and proxies into this socket" — the legacy TCP-shim model. If xray dials the UDS directly, that TCP-listen step (and the per-user port) is what we're eliminating, so `port` becomes vestigial/a hint. Confirm exact xray UDS config form (Domain Socket / dialing `path`) when wiring.

**Gemma (`op-gemma`) is the authoritative route generator at the front of this pipeline.** It's a oneshot s6 service (`deploy/s6/gemma/shell_up` runs `target/debug/op-gemma`): generates **subid → tag → xray + OpenFlow rules**, writes `/dev/shm/xray-routes.json` (`XrayRoute{tag, subdomains, GemmaBackend::{Unix{path}|Grpc|Tcp|Dns|Ingress}}`), then runs the identity shuttle (`run_schema_shuttle`) to regenerate `/dev/shm/xray-ghostbridge.json`. `gbr-xray` has `dependencies.d/gemma` so xray waits for it. In the shuttle, **Gemma routes take precedence**; legacy `UNIX_SOCKET_ENDPOINTS` only fills tags Gemma didn't supply. Pipeline: `op-gemma → xray-routes.json → run_schema_shuttle → xray-ghostbridge.json → gbr-xray`. NOTE current live state: `/dev/shm/xray-routes.json` absent + op-gemma not running → xray is on the STATIC `/etc/xray/config.json` fallback (legacy per-service TCP redirects, `abstract:false`); the dynamic domain-routing + domainsocket path is built but not active. The abstract-socket change belongs in what Gemma emits (`GemmaBackend::Unix{path}` → abstract) + `schema_bridge.rs` outbound builder.

**Domain routing is the mechanism (confirmed live + in generator), and it was a required switch:** with one shared port (`:443`), port/IP routing can't distinguish containers — every connection lands on the same listener. The only discriminator is the sniffed SNI hostname, so routing MUST be by `domain`. Live `/etc/xray/config.json` and `schema_bridge.rs` both set: every inbound `sniffing.enabled=true` + `destOverride:["tls","http","quic"]` + `routeOnly=true`; `routing.domainStrategy="AsIs"`; rules `{"type":"field","domain":[…],"outboundTag":"to-<label>"}`. `routeOnly:true` = use sniffed name only to pick the outbound, don't rewrite the destination. Adding a user = one domain rule + one `to-<label>` domainsocket outbound in `/dev/shm`, regenerated by the shuttle.

Related: [[unix-socket-plugin]] design; SNI demux requires TLS (plaintext mqtt 1883 has no SNI → use 8883 or a fixed internal route).
